subject: A meta analysis incorporating individual study uncertainty without raw data

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: A meta analysis incorporating individual study uncertainty without raw data
parts:
Hi,

I am currently working on a meta analysis of an aspect of the epidemiology of malaria. For those that are interested I am looking at the duration of the extrinsic incubation period (EIP; the time after a mosquito becomes infected with the parasite before it can transmit the parasite to a human).

The individual studies tend not to have the data that was used to form their estimates of EIP, but sometimes have an uncertainty associated with the quantity. For example they may quote EIP = 10 days +- 1 day. 

As I said this is sometimes the case, although not always. As common is to just quote the point estimate of EIP = 10 days.

My question is, does anyone have any bright ideas as to how I could bring together this heterogeneous data in a meta analysis? I'm assuming that I'll use a hierarchical model, where the individual EIPs, and their uncertainties, are drawn from a population-level distribution. However I am not really clear what form the model should take, and how it can be sufficiently flexible to encompass both types of aforementioned data -- that with uncertainty and that without.

One idea is to assume the individual study data -- both the point estimate and the uncertainty parameterise the mean and sd of a normal distribution. However I can't really see how this helps.

Any references to relevant literature would also be most welcome! Having trouble finding comparable studies.

Best,

Ben

messages.author: c02e0f9087e29020
messages.subject: Re: A meta analysis incorporating individual study uncertainty without raw data
parts:
Hi Ben, 

With Stan there is little complication in fitting a model without the raw data (see the '8 schools' example), so if you believe the uncertainty estimates given, then you are good to go. If the studies just give you summary statistics (e.g "+- 1 day." --> is that a confidence interval?), you would need to assume a probability model to apply it (e.g the Normal example you describe)

Where uncertainty estimates are not given, it seems to me you could treat this as a missing data problem. On this list you should find examples of how people have dealt with missing data. If all studies report sample size, it might be reasonable to assume the underlying sd of data from different studies is the same, and then the missing uncertainty estimates can be predicted from the 'complete data' studies as a function of sqrt(sample size). However, is it reasonable to assume that the missing uncertainty estimates are missing-at-random?  If there is some signal in the fact that uncertainty is not reported (ie studies without uncertainty estimates mix some valid results with some rubbish), then it might be better to leave these results out.

Anyway, as they say about free advice, it may be worth exactly what you paid for it...

messages.author: 0c58851d0882c770
messages.subject: Re: A meta analysis incorporating individual study uncertainty without raw data
parts:
From what you have sketched out, an idea going back to RA Fisher might be helpful - ignore the estimated within study uncertainty and take the study estimate as a number (this can be seen as a non-parametric random effects model ( Valid inference in random effects meta-analysis. Follmann DA, Proschan MA.). 

Now epidemiology suggests there will be important confounding and biases to deal with? 

(If so there is pretty much only this crappy old book chapter that I am aware of the directly discusses those issues Greenland S, O' Rourke K: Meta-Analysis. Page 652 in Modern Epidemiology, 3rd ed. Edited by Rothman KJ, Greenland S, Lash T. Lippincott Williams and Wilkins; 2008. )

Good luck,
Keith
